How to Run a Marketing RFP Without Wasting a Quarter

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 1 September 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

A long agency RFP often rewards polished proposals rather than the team most likely to solve the problem, and it costs more than most buyers realise. The ANA and 4A's estimated in 2023 that a typical US agency review with three finalists costs about $1 million across the client and the agencies, and the European agency association found the average agency spends about €43,800 on each new-business pitch. A good RFP describes the real situation and outcome, asks for approach and evidence rather than free work, and weights category experience and incentives over polish. For most companies below enterprise scale, a short brief, a few conversations and a paid first engagement find the partner faster.

A request for proposals (RFP) is a formal process for selecting a vendor: the company describes what it needs, several candidates respond with proposals, and the company chooses. For marketing partners it is common at larger companies and increasingly at smaller ones that want to appear disciplined.

Most marketing RFPs select for the firm best at writing proposals. That is a different skill from the one being bought.

What a pitch actually costs

The cost is usually invisible to the buyer, because most of it sits on the agencies' side. The ANA and 4A's interviewed more than 300 US marketers and agency executives in March 2023. They estimated a client spends about $374,000 to $409,000 running a review, a non-incumbent agency about $204,000 to compete, and an incumbent defending the account about $406,000. With three finalists, the total reached about $1 million without an incumbent and $1.2 million with one. Those figures come from large US advertisers, but the structure applies at every size.

In Europe, the European Association of Communications Agencies surveyed 412 agencies in 2025. The average agency spent about €651,000 a year on pitching, with teams of five to eight people each contributing over 44 hours per pitch. Only four in ten winning creative ideas were implemented by the client. To cover its annual pitching cost at a 10% EBITDA margin, an agency would need at least €7 million in won business.

That cost does not vanish. It is recovered in fees, from you or from other clients. A process that demands more unpaid work than the decision needs makes every candidate more expensive.

What an RFP should contain

The situation. What the company does, for whom, where it is commercially, and what has been tried. Include the uncomfortable parts: the rejected ad accounts, the channel that stopped working, the budget that was cut. Candidates who know the real situation propose real things.

The outcome sought. Stated as a business result over a time frame, not as a list of services. "Reduce cost per funded account by a third within two quarters" invites strategy. "Provide paid social management" invites a rate card.

The constraints. Budget range, timeline, category restrictions, compliance requirements, internal resources, and what the company will not do.

What is asked of respondents. Specific, limited, and answerable in a few pages: how they would approach the outcome, who would do the work, relevant experience in this category, how they are paid, and what they would need from the company.

How the decision will be made. Criteria, weights, timeline, and who decides.

The industry bodies say the same about briefing. The ANA and 4A's guidelines warn that a review without a thorough brief risks "garbage in, garbage out", and recommend a brief at every phase with detail increasing as the field narrows. The WFA and Agency Mania Solutions study of 69 multinationals, reported in September and October 2026, found advertisers scored a good brief at 5.6 out of 6 as a driver of agency performance, well above financial incentives at 3.9. The brief is the cheapest performance lever the buyer has.

SectionWhat it must sayWhat weak responses reveal
SituationReal position, including what failedGeneric plans that ignore the failures
OutcomeA business result and a time frameService lists and rate cards
ConstraintsBudget range, restrictions, compliance, resourcesPlans that need a budget you do not have
AskApproach, team, category evidence, fees, dependenciesLong credentials, little on your problem
DecisionCriteria, weights, timeline, deciderLobbying the wrong person

What to leave out

Requests for free strategy. An RFP that asks candidates to produce a full plan, a media plan, or a creative concept is asking for unpaid work, and the firms that comply are recovering the cost from other clients or will recover it from you. The good ones increasingly decline. Ask for approach and evidence, not for the deliverable. EACA's own recommendation is that agency selection should start with credentials and case studies before any speculative strategic or creative work, and the UK's IPA asks clients to screen "the right number of agencies, at clearly defined stages" without asking them to incur excessive costs.

Long questionnaires about company history, insurance, and diversity policies before shortlisting. Collect those from the finalists.

How to evaluate responses

Weight relevant category experience heavily, particularly for restricted categories, where a firm that has never had an account rejected will learn on your budget. Read the fee structure for the incentive it creates; our guide to how marketing services are priced sets out what each model rewards. Look for what the response declines to do; a firm that says "we would not recommend X for you" has thought about you. Discount polish. Check references by asking what went wrong and how the firm handled it. And meet the people who would actually do the work, not the people who sold it.

The ANA and 4A's cost study draws a further lesson: consider whether a review is needed at all. Its recommendations start with weighing alternatives to a review and investing in the existing relationship, because the disruption and delay are costs too. If the current partner has never had a clear brief, write one before replacing them.

Never award a significant engagement on the strength of a document. Award a small one, and let the work make the case for the next.

A shorter process that works better

For most companies below enterprise scale, a full RFP is more process than the decision needs. The alternative: a two-page brief covering situation, outcome, constraints, and budget range, sent to three to five candidates identified by reference and by evidence of category experience. A forty-five-minute conversation with each. A short written approach from the two or three that were credible, no free deliverables. Then a paid, scoped first engagement, a diagnostic with a defined end and a written output, with the preferred candidate, priced so that walking away is easy.

Full RFPShorter process
DurationAbout a quarterAbout three weeks
CandidatesLong list, then finalistsThree to five by reference and category evidence
What candidates produceLong proposals, often speculative workA conversation and a short written approach
What the buyer learnsWho writes the best documentHow the firm works on your actual problem
Final stepAward the full scopeA paid, scoped first engagement

That process takes three weeks rather than a quarter, produces evidence rather than proposals, and selects for the firm that does the work rather than the firm that describes it. Our explainer on what a distribution diagnostic is sets out what that first engagement should contain, and our piece on proposal standards covers what a good written response looks like from the seller's side.

The one rule

Never award a significant engagement on the strength of a document. Award a small one, and let the work make the case for the next.

lowob takeaways

  • Describe the business problem. Situation, outcome and constraints, not only a service list.
  • Do not ask for free work. Ask for approach, evidence and the actual team.
  • Brief well. Advertisers rate a good brief far above incentives as a driver of agency performance.
  • Use a paid first engagement. Let a small piece of real work decide the large one.

Common questions

What should a marketing agency RFP include?

The real situation, including what has failed; the outcome sought as a business result over a time frame; constraints such as budget range and category restrictions; a short, specific ask of respondents; and how the decision will be made.

How much does an agency pitch cost?

An ANA and 4A's study in 2023 estimated about $1 million in total for a typical US review with three finalists, split between client and agencies. EACA found European agencies spend about €43,800 on an average new-business pitch.

Should agencies be paid for pitch work?

If you ask for strategy, plans or creative concepts, you are asking for real work. Either pay for it or ask instead for approach and evidence, then pay for a scoped first engagement with the preferred firm.

How long should an agency selection process take?

For most companies below enterprise scale, about three weeks: a two-page brief, conversations with three to five candidates, short written approaches from two or three, and a paid first engagement.

Next move

Write the two-page brief before you contact any agency: situation, outcome, constraints and budget range. If you cannot state the outcome as a business result with a time frame, fix that first; no selection process will compensate for it.
